Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 7–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder, if you do not know﴾ and so on.

Concerning who they are, there are three views. The first: they are the people of the Torah and the Gospel; this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: they are the scholars of the Muslims; this was said by ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

The third: they are the believers among the People of the Book; this was said by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make them bodies that eat no food﴾ and so on.

Concerning this, there are two views. The first: its meaning is, "We did not make the prophets before you bodies that do not eat food and do not die, so that We would make you like that." This is because of their saying: ﴿This is not but a human like you﴾ [al-Muminun: 24]. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: "We only made them bodies that eat food, and they were not immortal; therefore We made you a body like them." This was said by Qatadah.

Al-Kalbi said: Or the "body" is that which has a soul and eats and drinks. According to this statement, that which does not eat or drink is a jism (a body or substance).

Mujahid said: The "jasad" is that which does not eat or drink. According to this statement, that which eats and drinks is a nafs (a soul or self).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 16–20:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Had We wished to take a pastime﴾ has three interpretations. The first: a child (walad). This is said by al-Hasan.

The second: that the pastime (lahw) is women. This is said by Mujahid.

Qatadah said: "The pastime, in the language of the people of Yemen, is the woman."

Ibn Jurayj said: "Because they said: Maryam is His consort and Isa is His son."

The third: that it is the pastime which is the caller of desire and the enticer of lust, as the poet said:

"It makes me desire the pastime, that I do not love it, and for the pastime there is a caller, intelligent and not heedless."

﴿Surely We would have taken it from Our presence⦆, that is, from Our own presence, if We were doers.

Ibn Jurayj said: "We would have taken wives and a child from the inhabitants of the heavens, and We have not taken from the inhabitants of the earth."

﴿If We were doers⦆ has two aspects. The first: "and We were not doers." This is said by Ibn Jurayj.

The second: that it has come in the sense of a conditional, and the sense of the statement is: "Were We to take it, We would take it in such a way that its knowledge does not reach you."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth upon falsehood, so it crushes it⦆ has three sayings. The first: the truth is the speech that is followed, and the falsehood is that which is repelled.

The meaning of "it crushes it" (yadmaghuhu) is that it destroys it and annihilates it, like the one struck on the head whose skull is smashed, so that it leads to his destruction.

The second: the truth is the Qur'an, and the falsehood is Iblis.

The third: the truth is admonitions and the falsehood is sins. This is said by some of the people of insight (ahl al-khawatir).

It may also be a fourth: the truth is Islam and the falsehood is shirk.

﴿Then it vanishes⦆ has two aspects. The first: "perishing." This is said by Qatadah.

The second: "departing." This is said by Ibn Shajarah.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they do not tire⦆ has four interpretations. The first: they do not grow weary. This is said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: they do not become exhausted. This is said by Qatadah.

The third: they do not disdain. This is said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: they do not cease, derived from al-hasir, which is the camel that has been cut off by exhaustion. The poet said:

"Upon it are the carcasses of the exhausted, but as for their bones, they are white, and as for their hides, they are hard."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 30–33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That the heavens and the earth were a closed mass, and We parted them﴾ There are three interpretations concerning this.

The first: the heavens and the earth were joined together, and God parted them by means of the air. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the heavens were a single closed, sealed mass, and God split them into seven heavens; and the earth was likewise, and He split it into seven earths. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: the heavens were a closed mass that did not rain, and the earth was a closed mass that did not produce plants; so He split the sky by rain and the earth by vegetation. This is the view of 'Ikrimah, 'Atiyyah, and Ibn Zayd.

Al-ratq (ratq) is closing or sealing, and al-fatq (fatq) is splitting or opening, and the two are opposites. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan said:

It is easy for them when they become angry, the wrath of the enemies and their humbling,
and the closing of breaches and the opening of what is sealed, and the undoing of affairs and their tightening.

﴿And We made from water every living thing﴾ There are three sayings concerning this. The first: the creation of every living thing is from water. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: the preservation of the life of every living thing is by water. This is also the view of Qatadah.

The third: and We made every living thing from the water of the loins (sulb). This is the view of Qutrub.

﴿Will they not then believe?﴾ That is: will they not affirm what they witness?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with them﴾ Al-rawasi are the mountains, and concerning their being so named there are two explanations:

(p-445) The first: because they are fixed firmly in the earth and stabilized. The poet said:

Its root has taken hold beneath the soil, and it has risen high toward the stars, a branch that never ceases to be tall.

The second: because the earth was made firm and stable by them.

Concerning al-rawasi among the mountains there are two sayings. The first: they are the fixed ones (al-thawabit); this is the view of Qutrub. The second: they are the heavy ones (al-thiqal); this is the view of al-Kalbi.

﴿Lest it should shake with them﴾ has two meanings. The first: lest it should move away with them. The second: lest it should convulse with them.

Al-mayd is agitation.

﴿And We made in it broad roads as paths﴾ Concerning al-fijaj there are two meanings. The first: they are the landmarks by which one is guided. The second: al-fijaj is the plural of fajj, which is a wide road between two mountains. Al-Kumayt said:

The paths grow narrow for us, though they are wide roads, and we do not know their waters, the peaceful and hidden.

﴿That perhaps they may be guided﴾ has two meanings. The first: they are paths of reflection, so that by reflecting upon them they may be guided to their religion. The second: they are routes by which they may be guided to the roads of their lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ There are three aspects concerning this. The first: protected from falling upon the earth. The second: protected from the devils; this is the view of al-Farra'. The third: in the sense of raised; this is the view of Mujahid.

It may also admit a fourth: protected from shirk and sins.

His saying, exalted and mighty is He: ﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; each in an orbit they swim﴾ There are two sayings concerning this. The first: the falak is the sky; this is the view of al-Suddi.

(p-446) The second: the falak is the revolving axis encircling what is in it of the sun, the moon, and the stars, and from it the spindle-whorl (falakat al-mighzal) was so named because of its rotation. The poet said:

She has been suffering the revolving orbit, until morning, working the spindle-threads.

Concerning the rotation of the falak there are two sayings. The first: it is like the turning of a ball. The second: it is like the turning of a millstone; this is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj.

Regarding the falak there are three sayings. The first: it is the sky, which turns with the sun, the moon, and the stars. The second: it is a rotating path within the sky in which the stars revolve while the sky remains fixed; this is the view of Qatadah. The third: it is a rotating path between the sky and the earth in which the stars revolve; this is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

﴿Swim﴾ has two meanings. The first: they are drawn along; this is the view of Mujahid. The second: they revolve; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. On the first meaning, the falak is what moves them; on the second, they are what revolve within the falak.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 34–35:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We test you with evil and with good as a trial﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations.

The first: [the evil and the good are] adversity and ease. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the evil is poverty and sickness, and the good is wealth and health. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

(p-447) The third: the evil is the dominance of desire over the self, and the good is protection (ʿismah) from acts of disobedience. This is the view of al-Tustari.

[It is] so that We may know your gratitude for what you love, and your patience with what you dislike. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Regarding the word ﴿trial﴾ (fitnah), there are two interpretations: the first is "testing" (ikhtiban).

The second is "probation" (ibtila').

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 36–40:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: the one meant by "man" is Adam. On this view, regarding His saying ﴿of haste﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: i.e., hastened before the sunset of Friday, which is the last of the six days. This was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: that he asked his Lord, after his form had been completed and the spirit had been breathed into his eyes and tongue, that his creation be hastened to completion and that the spirit be made to run through his whole body. This was said by al-Kalbi.

The third: that the meaning of ﴿of haste﴾ is i.e., of clay. From this is the saying of the poet: (p-448)

؎ The acacia-wood grows in the hard, smooth rock, and the palm grows between water and clay ('ajal).

The second opinion: the one meant by "man" is all of mankind. On this view, regarding His saying ﴿of haste﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: meaning that man was created hasty (ʿajūlan). This was said by Qatadah.

The second: haste was created in man. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: meaning that he was created with a love of haste.

Haste (al-ʿajalah) is putting a thing before its time, while swiftness (al-sur'ah) is doing it at the very beginning of its times.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verse 41–43:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say, "Who protects you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?"﴾ and the rest of the verse.

That is, who preserves you. Ibn Hirmah said:

Indeed Sulayma, and Allah is her guardian, has withheld something that would not diminish her.

The form of the expression is that of a question, but what is intended is negation. Its implied meaning is: Say, "There is no guardian for you by night and by day from the Most Merciful."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor will they be given companionship from Us.﴾ In it there are four interpretations:

The first: they will not be protected (yujaroon). This is related from Ibn Abbas, from their saying, "Indeed for you from so-and-so is a companion," meaning a protector (mujir). The poet said:

He calls out with the highest of his voice, seeking refuge, so that he may be given protection from them while the spears are reaching toward him.

The second: they will be guarded (yuhfazoon). This is related from Mujahid.

(p-449) The third: they will be helped (yunsaroon). This is transmitted on authority (ma'thur).

The fourth: they will not be given companionship from Allah with any good. This is related from Qatadah.

Al-Mawardi's commentary on Surah al-Anbiya' (21), verses 64–67, from *al-Nukat wa al-Uyun* (p-453):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they turned back to themselves﴾. On this there are two views. The first is that some of them turned back to others among them.

The second is that each one of them turned back to himself, reflecting on what Ibrahim (Abraham) had said. They were bewildered as to the answer he intended, so Allah, exalted is He, caused the truth to be spoken through their tongues, and ﴿they said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers"﴾, meaning in your questioning. For if these were gods, Ibrahim would not have been able to break them. Had they been granted success, they would have believed with this answer, because the truth became manifest in it upon their tongues.

﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads﴾. On this there are three views. The first is that its meaning is that they returned to their polytheism after acknowledging the truth.

The second: it means that they returned to their argument against Ibrahim, with their saying: ﴿"You certainly know that these do not speak"﴾.

The third: they were overturned upon their heads, and this could be one of two things from them: either humiliation due to the cutting off of their proof, or reflection upon their answer. Then Allah caused them to speak afterward with the proof, submitting to it and affirming it, by their saying: ﴿"You certainly know that these do not speak"﴾. So Ibrahim answered them after they had acknowledged the proof.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the tillage﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it was a field of crops into which the sheep of the people strayed at night. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: it was a vineyard whose grape clusters had grown. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Shurayh.

﴿When the sheep of the people strayed into it.﴾ Qatadah said: the nafsh is grazing at night, and the hamal is grazing by day. The poet said:

"Clinging to the outskirts of the houses, straying in the evening dust."

(p-457) ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon.﴾ Regarding their judgment there are two opinions. The first: it was in agreement, and they did not differ concerning it, because when God praised them He indicated their agreement on what is correct. And the saying of Him, Blessed and Exalted: ﴿So We gave understanding of it﴾ may be taken to mean that it was a virtue for him over David, because he was given judgment in his youth while David was given judgment in his old age, even though they both agreed on it and did not differ concerning it; because the prophets are protected from error and mistake, so that doubt does not fall upon their affairs and rulings. This is an anomalous view among the theologians.

The second opinion, which is the view of the majority of scholars and exegetes, is that their judgment differed: Solomon was correct in it, and David erred. As for the judgment of Solomon, he ruled for the owner of the tillage. As for the judgment of David, he saw that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the tillage so that he might benefit from their milk and offspring, and the tillage should be handed over to the owner of the sheep so that he might take charge of its cultivation. Then, when in the following year it returned to its former state, the sheep would be returned to their owner and the tillage returned to its owner. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid.

So David returned to the judgment of Solomon and ruled accordingly. Then God, Exalted, said: ﴿So We gave understanding of it to Solomon﴾, and He made the truth to be with him in his judgment. It is not impossible for error and mistake to occur from the prophets, just as it occurs from others.

However, they are not left to persist in it, even if others may persist in it; so that God may return the realities to them rather than to His creation; and for this reason they are called "the truth" and are distinguished thereby from the creation.

Those who held this view differed on whether it applies generally to all prophets, in two opinions. The first: our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is singled out from among them in that error is not permitted for him, but is permitted for the others. This was said by Abu 'Ali ibn Abi Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who distinguished him from all the other prophets, because he is the Seal of the Prophets, so there was no one after him to correct his error; and for this reason Allah protected him from it. Whereas after other prophets there came those who corrected their errors.

The second opinion: it applies generally to all prophets, and our Prophet and the other prophets are equal in the permissibility of error; except that they are not left to persist in it, and so the correction of those after them is not considered in it. Thus the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when a woman asked him about the 'iddah, said to her: "Observe the 'iddah wherever you wish." Then he said: "Glory be to Allah, remain in your house until the prescribed term reaches its end." And a man said: "What do you think, if I am killed patiently, seeking reward, will anything keep me from Paradise?" He said: "No." Then he called him back and said: "Except debt, as Jibril told me." And nothing is attributed to him except what is permissible for him.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. Al-Hasan said: Were it not for this verse, I would have thought that judges had perished; but He praised Solomon for his correctness and excused David for his ijtihad.

If it is said: how did David annul his judgment in favour of Solomon's ijtihad? The answer to this is from two aspects. The first: it is possible that David stated his ruling in absolute terms, and that was by way of a fatwa, so he stated it to them in order to bind them to it; then, when there appeared to him what was stronger in ijtihad than it, he returned to that.

The second: it is possible that God revealed this ruling to Solomon, so it was binding on him; and because of the explicit text that came by revelation, he saw fit to set aside his ijtihad, since a judge must set aside his ruling by ijtihad when it contradicts an explicit text.

Moreover, the scholars have differed concerning the prophets: is ijtihad permissible for them in rulings? A group said it is permissible for them to exercise ijtihad, for two reasons. The first: ijtihad is a virtue, and it is not proper that the prophets be deprived of it. (p-459) The second: ijtihad is stronger, so it was dearer to them, and they are more worthy of being bound by a ruling reached through it. This is the view of those who permit the prophets to err.

The others said: it is not permissible for the prophets to exercise ijtihad in rulings, because ijtihad is resorted to by the judge only for lack of an explicit text, and the prophets are not without an explicit text, since revelation descends upon them. Therefore ijtihad was not for them. This is the view of those who hold that the prophets are protected from error and mistake.

As for what our Law has settled concerning damage done by animals to crops: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib related that the she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib entered an orchard and damaged it, so the Prophet ﷺ ruled that owners of livestock must guard their animals at night, and owners of orchards must guard their orchards by day. Thus what animals damage at night is liable for compensation, and what they damage by day is not liable, because guarding them is burdensome for their owners, while it is not burdensome for them to guard them by day. So guarding at night became obligatory upon the owners of livestock, and they bear liability for what their livestock damage; and guarding by day became obligatory upon the owners of crops, so he did not rule in their favour for compensation for their crops, despite their negligence. This is among the most correct judgments and the most just rulings, showing mercy to both parties and ease to both groups. This does not contradict what David and Solomon, peace be upon them, ruled regarding the principle of liability, because they ruled it concerning grazing at night; and it differs only in its description, for in our Law the crop is liable for compensation, since they ruled that it be compensated for its loss, whether by excess or deficiency; and the harm of the animals does not arise when the compensation reaches the one entitled to it.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And to each We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. It may bear two meanings. The first: He gave each of them judgment and knowledge similar to what He gave the other. Regarding the intended meaning of judgment and knowledge there are two possible views: the first, that judgment is adjudication and knowledge is fatwa. The second, that judgment is ijtihad and knowledge is explicit text.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with David﴾. It may bear two meanings: the first: We made them submissive. The second: We inspired them.

﴿And the birds.﴾ Regarding their glorification there are three views. The first: their travelling with him is their glorification; this was said by Ibn 'Isa, and tasbih (glorification) is derived from sibahah (swimming/gliding). The second: their prayers with him; this was said by Qatadah. The third: it is an audible glorification which he understood; this is the view of Yahya ibn Salam.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: labus is the coat of mail that is worn; this was said by Qatadah. The second: among the Arabs, all weapons are called labus.

﴿To protect you from your violence.﴾ Regarding this there are two views. The first: from your weapons; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: from the war of your enemies; this was said by al-Dahhak.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to Solomon [We subjected] the wind, violent, blowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed.﴾ Its meaning: We subjected the wind to Solomon. 'Usuf means the intensity of its movement, and 'asf means chaff; the intensity of the wind was named after it because it grinds it with its fierce force.

﴿Blowing by his command toward the land which We had blessed.﴾ That is the land of Syria. Regarding its blessing there are three sayings. The first: because of the prophets sent there. The second: because the waters of the land's rivers flow from it. The third: because of the goodness God deposited in it; this was said by Qatadah: whatever is lacking from the land is supplied in the land of Syria, and whatever is lacking in Syria is supplied in Palestine; and it was said that it is the land of the gathering and the dispersal.

(p-461) The wind used to carry Solomon and his companions wherever he wished.

Muqatil said: Solomon was the first to extract pearls by means of the diving of the devils.

He said: "From the side of his wife." They said: "Then deal with Job through his wife."

She came to Job, cried out and said: "O Job, how long will your Lord torment you and not have mercy on you? Where is the wealth? Where are the children? Where is your fine complexion? It has decayed, and the creatures have spread over you. Slaughter this goat and find rest."

The fourth: he rose to pray but could not stand up, so he said: "adversity has touched me," informing of his state, not complaining of his affliction; this was narrated by Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

The fifth: revelation was cut off from him for forty days, so he feared the abandonment of his Lord, and he said: "adversity has touched me." This is the saying of Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah have mercy on him.

Concerning the form of his saying ﴿adversity has touched me﴾ there are four views. The first: it is in the form of a question, its sense being: "Does adversity touch me, when You are the Most Merciful of the merciful?"

The second: "You are more merciful to me than that adversity should touch me."

The third: he said it seeking to be excused from his sin and desiring his Lord.

The fourth: he complained of his weakness and his harm, seeking the tenderness of His mercy. So He removed his affliction, and it was said to him: ﴿Strike with your foot; this is a cool bath and a drink﴾ [38:42]. He struck with his foot, a spring gushed forth, he washed in it and drank from it, the inner part of his illness departed, his youth and beauty returned to him, he stood up healthy, and Allah multiplied for him what he had had of family, wealth and children.

Then his wife said: "If he has driven me away, to whom shall I entrust him?" She returned but did not see him, and began to wander and weep, while Job saw her and she saw him, yet she did not recognize him. When she asked him about him and spoke with him, she recognized him. Then Allah had mercy on her for her patience with him in the affliction, and commanded him to strike her with a bundle (of grass) so that he would fulfill his oath. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

His wife was Makhira, daughter of Misha, son of Yusuf, son of Ya'qub.

The Qur'anic words: **Dhu al-Nun** (﴿وَذا النُّونِ﴾) is Yunus ibn Matta, and he was so called because he was the companion of the fish, as God the Exalted says: ﴿And be not like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48]. The fish is *al-nun*, and he was named after it because it swallowed him. The poet says:

؎ O finest of castles, how excellent the castle and the valley,
and how fine its people, from the settled and the nomad.
∗∗∗ Its pools are full, and the wild beasts graze in it,
and the lizard, the *nun* (fish), the sailor and the driver.

He means that in it are gathered the game of land and sea, the people of wealth and of the camel-herd, and the people of the desert and the settled life.

﴿When he went off in anger﴾. There are three opinions about this:

First: he meant that he was defiant toward the king, whose name was Hizqiya, though there was no harm in him. This is related by al-Naqqash.

Second: he was angry with his people. This is said by al-Hasan.

Third: he was angry with his Lord. This is said by al-Sha'bi. His anger was not defiance, because defiance of God is disbelief, which is not permissible for the prophets. Rather, it was his leaving without permission, and that was his disobedience.

Regarding the reason for his going to his people, there are two views:

(p-466) One: there was a narrowness in his disposition, and when the weight of prophethood was laid upon him, his patience was strained and he did not endure it. God also said: ﴿So be patient as the steadfast messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. This is said by Wahb.

Two: it was the custom of his people that whoever lied, they would kill him, and they had never found him to lie. So when he informed them that punishment would descend upon them, and God lifted it from them, he said: "I will not return to them as a liar," and he feared they would kill him, so he went out fleeing.

﴿So he thought that We would not decree against him﴾. There are four interpretations:

First: he thought that We would not restrict his paths. From this is His saying: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7], meaning, whose provision is narrowed. This is said by Ibn Abbas.

Second: he thought that We would not punish him for what he had done. This is said by Qatada and Mujahid.

Third: he thought that We would not judge against him by what We had judged. This is related by Ibn Shajara. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "We would not decree upon him the punishment that We had decreed," taken from *al-qadr*, which means judgment and not power. Ibn Abbas read *nuqaddir* with the doubled letter, which is the meaning mentioned by al-Farra'. It cannot be taken to mean incapacity to have power over him, because that would be disbelief.

Fourth: it is in the sense of a question, its assumed form being: "Did he think that We would not have power over him?", and the alif of interrogation was deleted for brevity. This is said by Sulayman ibn al-Mu'tamir.

﴿So he called out in the darknesses﴾. There are two views:

One: they are the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the belly of the fish. This is said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada.

Two: they are the darkness of the fish within the belly of the fish. This is said by Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd.

It may also carry a third meaning: the darkness of sin, the darkness of hardship, and the darkness of loneliness.

(p-467) ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers﴾. That is, against myself, in leaving without Your permission. This was not a punishment from God, because the prophets may not be punished. It was rather a discipline, and one may be disciplined even if he does not deserve punishment, as with children.

God the Exalted says: ﴿So We answered him﴾. Regarding the answering of supplication there are two views:

One: it is a reward from God to the one who supplicates, and it cannot be other than a reward.

Two: it is a means of setting things right, so it may be a reward, and it may be other than a reward.

﴿And We delivered him from the distress﴾. This may have two meanings:

One: from the distress caused by his sin.

Two: from the belly of the fish, because *al-ghamm* means covering.

It is said that God revealed to the fish that it should not break any of his bones nor scratch his skin.

When he was in its belly, he said: "O Lord, You have taken for me a place of worship in places that no one has ever taken."

As for the duration of his stay in the belly of the fish, there are three views:

One: forty days.

Two: three days.

Three: from the rising of the day until its end.

Al-Sha'bi said: four hours. Then the fish opened its mouth, and Yunus saw the light of the sun, and he said: "Glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers," and the fish spat him out.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 89–90:

﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone (fardan)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

(p-468) First: left bereft of Your protection (ʿiṣmah), as said by Ibn ʿAṭāʾ.

Second: turning away from Your obedience.

Third, and this is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur), i.e., alone, without a child.

﴿And You are the best of inheritors﴾, meaning: You are the best of those who inherit the servants, whether family or children. He intended by this that his longing toward God was for a child and family, not for wealth, but so that the child would be righteous and, in prophethood, would follow [him].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We answered him, and We gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. First: she had been barren, so she was made fertile.

al-Kalbi said: she bore him a child when he was in his seventies.

Second: her tongue had been long (i.e., she had a sharp or unruly tongue), so He granted her good character. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Kamil.

﴿They used to hasten to good deeds﴾, meaning they would race to righteous actions, referring to Zakariyya, his wife, and Yahya.

﴿And they called upon Us with longing and fear﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations: First: longing for Our reward and fear of Our punishment.

Second: longing for acts of obedience and fear of acts of disobedience.

Third: longing with the insides of the palms and fear with the backs of the palms.

Fourth: meaning hope and fear.

It may also bear a fifth interpretation: longing for the good they strive for, and fear of the evil they seek to ward off.

﴿And they were humbly submissive to Us﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations: First: meaning humble, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

(p-469) Second: longing and fearing, and this is the view of al-Dahhak.

Third: that he placed the right hand upon the left and looked toward the place of prostration in prayer.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verse 91:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿who guarded her chastity﴾ has two interpretations. The first: she was chaste and refrained from immorality.

The second: the intended meaning of "chastity" (farj) is the opening (farj) of her garment, from which she prevented Jibril, before she knew that he was a messenger.

﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾, meaning: We caused the spirit of the Messiah to pass into her as air passes by blowing. He attributed the spirit to Himself as an honour to him. It has also been said that rather, He commanded Jibril, and he unfastened the collar of her garment with his fingers, then breathed into it, and she conceived from that very moment.

﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾, because she conceived without contact, and Jesus was born without a father, together with his speaking in the cradle, then his testifying to her innocence from immorality. So this was the sign. Al-Dahhak said: she gave birth to him on the day of 'Ashura'.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community﴾. Its meaning is that your religion is one religion. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

In my opinion it may also bear two other meanings. The first: you are one creation, so you should not be upon anything but one religion.

The second: you are people of one era, so you should not be upon anything but one religion.

﴿And I am your Lord, so worship Me﴾. Thus He commanded that none other than Him be worshipped.

﴿But they divided their affair among themselves﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: they differed concerning the religion; this was said by al-Akhfash.

The second: they separated into factions; this was said by al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 95–97:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And there is a prohibition upon a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations.

The first: its meaning is, "There is a prohibition upon a town which We found destroyed by sins, that they will not return to repentance." This is the saying of ʿIkrimah.

The second: "And there is a prohibition upon a town which We destroyed with punishment, that they will not return to the world." This is the saying of al-Hasan. Ibn ʿAbbas recited it as وَحَرُمَ عَلَى قَرْيَةٍ (wa-ḥaruma ʿalā qaryatin), and its interpretation is what Sufyan said: "It was obligatory upon a town which We destroyed."

[That they will not return: he said, they will not repent.]

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose﴾, meaning the barrier was opened. This is one of the portents of the Hour. Abu Hurayrah narrated from Zaynab bint Jahsh, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sleeping in his house, then he awoke with his eyes reddened, and he said: 'There is no god but Allah,' three times. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today there has been opened from the barrier of Gog and Magog the like of this," and he gestured with his hand to the formation of ninety.

As for Gog and Magog, it is said that they are two brothers, and they are sons of Japheth son of Noah. Regarding the derivation of their two names there are two views: the first is that it is derived from "ajjat al-nar" (the fire blazed). The second is from "al-ma' al-ujaj" (the bitter, scorching water).

It is also said that they multiply beyond mankind by double.

﴿And they will come swarming from every mound﴾. Regarding "ḥadab al-arḍ" (the mounds of the earth) there are three views: the first is that it means its wide tracks and its edges, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: around it.

The third: its hills and mounds, derived from "ḥadabat al-ẓahr" (the hump of the back). ʿAntarah said:

"My hands did not tremble, nor was I dismayed, by their coming upon me from the mounds."

Regarding His saying ﴿yansilūn﴾ there are two meanings: the first is that it means they go forth, and from this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"So take off your garments from your clothes, and let them slip off."

The second is that it means they hasten, and from this is the saying of the poet:

"The wolf's swift stride, when it came near, while the night grew cold upon it, so it sped on."

Regarding the phrase ﴿from every mound they swarm﴾ there are two views: the first is that they are Gog and Magog; this is the saying of Ibn Masʿud.

The second is that they are mankind, who will be gathered to the place of standing.

The second: its meaning is the firewood (hatab) of Hell. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and ʿAʾisha recited it as ḥaṭab Jahannam.

The third: they will be thrown into it as pebbles are thrown, until it seems that Hell is being pelted (tuḥaṣṣabu) with them. This is the saying of al-Ḍaḥḥak, and from it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us with a hail-stone like scattered cotton-fluff (kanadif al-qutn manthur).

He means snow. Ibn ʿAbbas recited ḥaḍab Jahannam, with the letter ḍad dotted.

Al-Kisa'i said: "You (ḥaḍḍabta) the fire with the dotted ḍad when you kindle it and throw into it what sets it alight of firewood."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (al-ḥusna) has preceded from Us﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: it is obedience to Allah, Exalted is He; this was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: it is happiness (saʿada) from Allah, and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is Paradise, and this is the saying of al-Suddi.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that it is repentance (tawba).

﴿Those will be kept far away from it﴾, meaning from Hell.

Concerning those (who are referred to) there are three opinions. The first: they are ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels who were worshipped besides Allah while they were averse to it. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: they are ʿUthman, Talha, and al-Zubayr. This was narrated by al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

The third: it is general to everyone for whom the best from Allah has preceded.

The third: it is when Hell closes over its inhabitants, and this is the saying of Ibn Jurayj.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that it is the presentation (ʿarḍ) at the place of gathering (al-maḥshar).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you and that which you worship other than Allah are the firewood of Hell﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: it is the fuel of Hell (wuqud Jahannam), and this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: its meaning is the firewood (hatab) of Hell. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and ʿAʾisha recited it as ḥaṭab Jahannam.

The third: they will be thrown into it as pebbles are thrown, until it seems that Hell is being pelted (tuḥaṣṣabu) with them. This is the saying of al-Ḍaḥḥak, and from it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Facing the north of Syria, it strikes us with a hail-stone like scattered cotton-fluff (kanadif al-qutn manthur).

He means snow. Ibn ʿAbbas recited ḥaḍab Jahannam, with the letter ḍad dotted.

Al-Kisa'i said: "You (ḥaḍḍabta) the fire with the dotted ḍad when you kindle it and throw into it what sets it alight of firewood."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (al-ḥusna) has preceded from Us﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: it is obedience to Allah, Exalted is He; this was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: it is happiness (saʿada) from Allah, and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is Paradise, and this is the saying of al-Suddi.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that it is repentance (tawba).

﴿Those will be kept far away from it﴾, meaning from Hell.

Concerning those (who are referred to) there are three opinions. The first: they are ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels who were worshipped besides Allah while they were averse to it. This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: they are ʿUthman, Talha, and al-Zubayr. This was narrated by al-Nuʿman ibn Bashir from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib.

The third: it is general to everyone for whom the best from Allah has preceded.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what is related: "When the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, you and that which you worship other than Allah are the firewood of Hell﴾ was revealed, the polytheists said: 'Then the Messiah, ʿUzayr, and the angels have also been worshipped.' So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us, those will be kept far away from it﴾," meaning from Hell. And His saying, ﴿Indeed, you and that which you worship other than Allah are the firewood of Hell﴾ is to be understood as referring to those whom their Lord punishes.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: the greatest terror is the final blast (al-nafkha al-akhira), and this is the saying of al-Ḥasan.

The second: it is the slaughter of death (dhabḥ al-mawt), related by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: it is when Hell closes over its inhabitants, and this is the saying of Ibn Jurayj.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that it is the presentation (ʿarḍ) at the place of gathering (al-maḥshar).

(p-474) His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day We shall roll up the heaven like the rolling of a scroll for writings﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

First: that al-Sijill is the page (ṣaḥīfah), which is rolled up along with what is written on it. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

Second: that it is an angel (malak).

Third: that it is a scribe who used to write in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 105–107:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And We have written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations.

(p-475) One: that the Zabur is the books which Allah the Exalted sent down to His prophets, and the Reminder is the Mother of the Book (Umm al-Kitab) which is with Him in the heaven. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: that the Zabur is among the books which Allah the Exalted sent down to the prophets after Musa. This is the view of al-Sha'bi.

﴿That the earth, My righteous servants shall inherit it﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. One: that it is the land of Paradise, which the people of obedience will inherit. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it is the Holy Land, which the Children of Israel will inherit. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

The third: that it is the land of this world, and the one who will inherit it is the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship﴾. As for His saying ﴿Indeed, in this﴾, there are two opinions. One of them: it means in the Qur'an.

The second: in this surah.

Regarding His saying ﴿a message for a people who worship﴾, there are two interpretations. One: that it is a message delivered to them which restrains them from disobedience and impels them to obedience.

The second: that it is a message for them which conveys them to the pleasure of Allah and His abundant reward.

Regarding His saying ﴿who worship﴾, there are two interpretations. One: obedient.

The second: knowing.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. Regarding what is meant by this mercy there are two interpretations. One: guidance to the obedience of Allah and deserving His reward.

(p-476) The second: that it is that the punishment of total destruction (al-isti'sal) was lifted from them.

Regarding His saying ﴿to the worlds﴾ there are two interpretations. One: those among them who believed, so it is particular to the believers if it is said that the mercy is guidance.

The second: all of them, so it is general to the believers and disbelievers if it is said that the mercy is that the punishment of total destruction was lifted from them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 21, verses 108–112:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Then if they turn away﴾ means they turn away. In this there are two interpretations. The first: away from you. The second: away from the Qur'an.

﴿Say: I have announced to you on an equal footing﴾ In this there are seven interpretations. The first: upon a clear and just matter. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The second: in due time (mahal). This is the saying of Qatadah.

The third: upon justice ('adl). This is the saying of al-Farra'.

The fourth: upon open declaration, not in secret. This is the saying of al-Kalbi.

The fifth: on an equal footing in the announcement, such that it does not appear to favour some of them over others. This is the saying of Ali ibn Isa.

The sixth: equality in faith in it (in belief in it).

The seventh: its meaning is that whoever disbelieves in it, they are equal in respect of fighting and striving against them. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿And I do not know whether it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: perhaps the delay of the punishment is a trial for you. The second: perhaps the lifting of the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal) is a trial for you.

Regarding this trial there are three views. The first: it is destruction for you. The second: it is a tribulation for you. The third: it is a kindness to you.

﴿And a provision for a time﴾ In this there are three sayings. The first: until the Day of Resurrection. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: until death. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The third: until the decree of God, may He be exalted, concerning them comes.

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿He said: My Lord, judge with truth.﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: hasten the judgment with truth.

The second: its meaning is: decide between us and the polytheists by that which makes the truth manifest to all. This is the meaning of the saying of Qatadah.

﴿And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one whose help is sought against what you describe.﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: against what you lie about. This is said by Qatadah.

The second: against what you conceal. This is said by al-Kalbi.

It has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he witnessed fighting, would recite this verse.

And God knows best.
